# Example
# And another example:

> At the onset of the monsoon, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew away to Lake Manasa <note>the sacred Manasarovar lake in the Himalayas</note>. One-eighth of the flock flew away from the water's edge to a forest of land-growing lotuses. O young girl! Three pairs of swans were seen playing with great passion in water adorned with young lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of the flock. (3)

**Syntax:** O young girl! At the onset of the monsoon, ten times the square root of the swan flock went to Manasa. One-eighth flew from the water's edge to a forest of land-growing lotuses. And three pairs of swans were seen eagerly engaged in play in water shining with young lotus stalks. Therefore, tell the total number of the flock. (3)

**Meaning:** O my beloved, sixteen years of age! There was a group of swans. When the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root of them went to Lake Manasarovar. One-eighth <note>1/8</note> of the flock flew from the shore into a forest of land-growing lotuses. Three pairs of swans <note>amounting to 6 birds</note> were seen playing very affectionately in water beautified by tender lotus roots. Then say, how many swans were in that group? (3)

**Layout of the calculation:** The square root multiplier is 10. The eighth part is <gloss>1/8</gloss>. The visible number is <gloss>6</gloss>. Since it was stated <note>in a previous rule</note> that the quantity is "reduced or increased by the fractions," here we divide the visible number and the square root multiplier by the remainder of the parts <note>1 minus 1/8, which is 7/8</note>. The resulting visible number is <gloss>48/7</gloss>. The square root multiplier is <gloss>80/7</gloss>. Half of this multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. The square of this <gloss>1600/49</gloss> plus the visible number <note>converted to 336/49</note> is <gloss>1936/49</gloss>. The square root of this is <gloss>44/7</gloss>. Adding half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and squaring the result, the quantity of swans is found: 144.

**Expansion:** According to the rule mentioned in the second verse <note>a previous mathematical rule for quadratic equations</note>, we subtract the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> from one <gloss>1/1 - 1/8</gloss> = <gloss>7/8</gloss>. This is used to divide the visible quantity of 6. <gloss>6/1 divided by 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>6/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>48/7</gloss>. Thus, <gloss>48/7</gloss> becomes the adjusted visible quantity <term>drishya rashi</term> <gloss>the known constant in the equation</gloss>. Similarly, we divide the square root multiplier of 10 by <gloss>7/8</gloss>. <gloss>10/1 divided by 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>10/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>80/7</gloss>. Thus, <gloss>80/7</gloss> becomes the adjusted square root multiplier <term>mula-guna</term>. Now, taking <gloss>48/7</gloss> as the visible quantity and <gloss>80/7</gloss> as the multiplier, we perform the operation according to the method in the verse above. That is, half the multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. The square of this is <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. Adding this to the visible quantity <gloss>48/7</gloss>...

<summary>This page presents a poetic mathematical problem involving a flock of swans to demonstrate solving quadratic equations. It provides the verse, a prose explanation, and a detailed step-by-step numerical solution resulting in the total count of 144 swans.</summary>

Vasudeva is the Supreme Brahman. His form is the Supreme Person; he is unmanifest, devoid of qualities, peaceful, beyond the twenty-five elements, and imperishable, meaning he is free from transformation. 12.

->The Deity, residing within nature and pervading all things both outside and inside, is Sankarshana. Having first created the waters, he cast his seed into them. 13.<-

Because the pure Brahman cannot be the direct cause of the material world, the author says: Residing within nature, meaning covered by <term>maya</term> <gloss>illusion</gloss>, and pervading all things both outside and inside because he is the material cause of the universe. All these attributes of Sankarshana, though he is a partial manifestation of Vasudeva, are to be understood as being essentially identical to Vasudeva. Sankarshana, as an aspect of Vasudeva, first created the waters. In those waters, he cast his seed, a specific potency. 13.

The deity Sankarshana, who is perceptible everywhere, entered into this very nature and first created water. Afterward, he established his own radiance in the form of a seed within that water. 13.

->That became a golden egg, surrounded everywhere by darkness. Within it, the eternal Aniruddha was first manifested. 14.<-

The author explains what happened next. That water, combined with that potency, became a golden, spherical egg, covered everywhere, both outside and inside, by darkness. The meaning is that the golden egg was produced in space accompanied by darkness. Within that golden egg, Aniruddha, the eternal and constant aspect of Sankarshana (himself an aspect of Vasudeva), first became manifest. He was not "born" or "created," but rather became manifest, following the doctrine of <term>satkaryavada</term> <gloss>the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause</gloss>. Just as oil is already present in sesame seeds and is merely made manifest, he was not newly produced. 14.

That seed-like radiance took the form of a golden egg. It was surrounded on all sides by darkness. There, within the egg, the eternal Lord Aniruddha first appeared. 14.

->He is celebrated in the Vedas as the Golden Embryo. He is called Aditya because he was manifest from the beginning, and Surya because of his progression. 15.<-

Now the author provides his other names for the easy understanding of the world. This Lord Aniruddha, an aspect of Sankarshana endowed with the six-fold divine attributes <note>original: "shadaigunya-aishvarya"</note>, is described in the <term>Chhandas</term> <gloss>Vedas</gloss> as <term>Hiranyagarbha</term> <gloss>Golden Embryo</gloss> because he resided within the interior of the golden egg. This is his famous alternative name in the Vedas. He is certainly called <term>Aditya</term> because he was the first to be manifest. He is called <term>Surya</term> <note>derived here from the root for "moving" or "proceeding"</note> because of his progression, as he is the one through whom this world is brought forth into manifestation.

The <term>Shruti</term> <gloss>scripture</gloss> says:
"In the beginning, the Golden Embryo evolved; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists." <note>Rig Veda 10.121.1</note> 15.

This is the Lord Hiranyagarbha mentioned in the Vedas. First...

From the root *hve* <note>to call</note> comes the suffix *ap* and vocalization of the semi-vowel. *Suktāni* <note>well-spoken/hymns</note>: derived from the prefix *su* <note>well</note> and the root *vac* <note>to speak</note> in the passive past participle. Because it follows the prefix *su*, the final syllable of the second member is accented. *Haryataṃ*: from the root *harya*, meaning to move or to desire, belonging to the first conjugation.

When Agni and Soma are the deities of the low-voiced sacrifice <note>upāṃśuyāja</note> during the full moon, the verse "O Agni and Soma, he who today..." is the invitatory verse <note>anuvākyā</note>. This is indicated in the section concerning the stated deities: "O Agni and Soma, he who today... Matariśvan brought the one from heaven" <note>Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.6</note>. He now states this second verse:

## Hymn Text

**O Agni and Soma, whoever today offers this word as service to you both, bestow upon him abundant heroic strength, the prosperity of cattle, and a wealth of good horses. || 2 ||**

->Word-for-Word Analysis<-
**अग्नीषोमा** <term>Agnīṣomā</term> <gloss>O Agni and Soma</gloss> | **यः** <term>yaḥ</term> <gloss>whoever</gloss> | **अद्य** <term>adya</term> <gloss>today</gloss> | **वाम्** <term>vām</term> <gloss>to you two</gloss> | **इदम्** <term>idam</term> <gloss>this</gloss> | **वचः** <term>vacaḥ</term> <gloss>word/speech</gloss> | **सपर्यति** <term>saparyati</term> <gloss>honors/serves</gloss> | **तस्मै** <term>tasmai</term> <gloss>to him</gloss> | **धत्तम्** <term>dhattam</term> <gloss>bestow/give</gloss> | **सु-वीर्यम्** <term>su-vīryam</term> <gloss>good heroic might</gloss> | **गवाम्** <term>gavām</term> <gloss>of cattle</gloss> | **पोषम्** <term>poṣam</term> <gloss>nourishment/increase</gloss> | **सु-अश्व्यम्** <term>su-aśvyam</term> <gloss>wealth in good horses</gloss> || 2 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma**, whatever **sacrificer today, in this ritual,** performs **service** or makes honored **this word** consisting of praise **for you both**, **bestow** or grant **to that** sacrificer the **increase of cattle** and livestock. What kind of increase? One **accompanied by good heroic strength** or power, and one **possessing good horses**. Regarding the word *gavām* <note>of cattle</note>: the usual accent on the case ending for monosyllabic roots is prohibited here by a specific grammatical rule regarding the words for cattle and horses.

## Hymn Text

**O Agni and Soma, whoever presents an oblation, or whoever offers the preparation of the sacrifice to you both, may he, through his progeny, attain excellent heroic strength and the full span of life. || 3 ||**

->Word-for-Word Analysis<-
**अग्नीषोमा** <term>Agnīṣomā</term> <gloss>O Agni and Soma</gloss> | **यः** <term>yaḥ</term> <gloss>whoever</gloss> | **आहुतिम्** <term>āhutim</term> <gloss>oblation</gloss> | **यः** <term>yaḥ</term> <gloss>whoever</gloss> | **वाम्** <term>vām</term> <gloss>to you two</gloss> | **दाशात्** <term>dāśāt</term> <gloss>should give</gloss> | **हविः-कृतिम्** <term>haviḥ-kṛtim</term> <gloss>the preparation of the offering</gloss> | **सः** <term>saḥ</term> <gloss>he</gloss> | **प्र-जया** <term>pra-jayā</term> <gloss>with offspring/progeny</gloss> | **सु-वीर्यम्** <term>su-vīryam</term> <gloss>good heroic might</gloss> | **विश्वम्** <term>viśvam</term> <gloss>all/whole</gloss> | **आयुः** <term>āyuḥ</term> <gloss>life-span</gloss> | **वि** <term>vi</term> <gloss>fully</gloss> | **अश्नवत्** <term>aśnavat</term> <gloss>may he attain</gloss> || 3 ||

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma, whatever sacrificer should give an oblation** such as clarified butter **to you both**, or **whoever** should give the **preparation of the offering** made with sacrificial cake or pot-ladle offerings, **may that** sacrificer **attain** or pervade the **whole span of life** accompanied by **progeny** such as sons and grandsons, and possessing **excellent heroic strength**. *Āhutim* <note>oblation</note>: derived from the root *hu* <note>to sacrifice</note> with the suffix *ktin*; the prefix retains its original accent. *Dāśāt*: from the root *dāś* <note>to give</note>; it uses the Vedic subjunctive mood with an inserted 'a' vowel. The accent is not dropped because of the connection with the relative pronoun *yat*. *Haviṣkṛtim*: the oblation in which the preparation of the offering occurs. In this compound, the first member retains its original accent.

<meta>The source text is a portion of Adi Shankaracharya's commentary on the Brahma Sutras, specifically discussing the nature of the soul during dreams and deep sleep (suşupti).</meta>

# But by meditating on the Supreme, that which is hidden is revealed, for from Him come the soul’s bondage and liberation. (3.2.5)

(3.2.5)

Now, it might be argued: the <term>jīva</term> <gloss>individual soul</gloss> is a part of the Supreme Self, just as a spark is a part of a fire. Since this is the case, just as the fire and the spark share the same powers of burning and lighting, so too the individual soul and the Lord should share the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Consequently, the soul, through its power of knowledge and sovereignty, should be able to create chariots and such in dreams merely by its will.

To this we reply: even though the individual soul and the Lord stand in the relation of part to whole, it is a matter of direct perception that the soul’s nature is opposite to that of the Lord.

But does this mean the soul does not possess the same nature as the Lord at all? No, that is not the case. Though it exists, that nature is hidden <note>original: "tirohita"</note> by the intervention of ignorance and other factors. This hidden nature is revealed only to someone who, through meditating on the Supreme Lord and putting forth effort, has wiped away their darkness—just as the power of sight, obscured by a cataract, is restored by the potency of medicine. This happens by the grace of the Lord to someone who has achieved perfection, not naturally to all living beings. Why? Because from Him, the Lord, come both the bondage and the liberation of this soul. Bondage arises from the lack of knowledge regarding the Lord's true nature, while liberation arises from the knowledge of that nature. Thus says the scripture: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the exhaustion of sufferings, birth and death cease. By meditating on Him, a third state is reached when the body is discarded—universal sovereignty—where one is absolute and has all desires fulfilled" <note>Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.11</note>, and so forth.

# Or, that hiding of nature also results from the connection with the body. (3.2.6)

(3.2.6)

But why does the soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty hidden? It would seem more logical for these powers not to be hidden, just as the burning and lighting powers of a spark are not hidden.

We reply: it is true; however, that hiding of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty results from its connection with the body—that is, its connection with the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the experience of objects. There is an analogy for this: just as the burning and lighting powers of a fire, though inherent, become hidden when the fire is latent in wood <note>original: "araṇi"</note> or covered by ash. In the same way, due to the connection with the limiting adjunct of the body—which is produced by Name and Form established through ignorance—the soul's knowledge and sovereignty are hidden by the delusion of failing to discriminate between the soul and the body.

The word "or" <note>original: "vā"</note> in the aphorism is intended to dispel the doubt that the soul is something other than the Lord. One might argue: let the soul be entirely different from the Lord because its knowledge and sovereignty are hidden; why invent the idea of a connection to a body? We say no, for the soul's difference from the Lord is not tenable. Starting with the passage "That divinity thought," the scripture refers to the soul with the word "Self" in "entering by means of this living soul <note>jīva</note> which is my Self." Furthermore, the scripture teaches the soul its identity with the Lord in the statement: "That is the Truth, That is the Self, That Thou Art, O Shvetaketu." Therefore, the soul is non-different from the Lord, but its knowledge and sovereignty are hidden by its connection to the body.

Because of this, it is not possible for the soul to create chariots and so forth in dreams merely by its will. If dream creation were subject to the soul's will, no one would ever see an unpleasant dream, for no one wills what is unpleasant for themselves. As for the argument that the scripture describes the dream state as being like the waking state to show its reality: that comparison is not intended to suggest reality, as that would contradict the soul's nature as "self-luminous" and the scriptural declaration that there are no actual chariots in dreams. Rather, since dreams are caused by the impressions <note>vāsana</note> arising from the waking state, the comparison merely indicates that the dream appears similar to it. Therefore, it is established that the dream is <term>māyā-mātra</term> <gloss>mere illusion</gloss>.

# The absence of that dream occurs in the channels and in the Self, according to scripture. (3.2.7)

**Section on the Absence of Dreams (Deep Sleep)** (3.2.7)

The state of dreaming has been examined; the state of deep sleep <term>suṣupti</term> is now examined. Regarding that, there are these scriptural passages concerning deep sleep. In one place it is said: "Now when he is thus asleep, composed, serene, and knows no dream, then he has entered these <term>nāḍī</term> <gloss>subtle channels</gloss>" <note>Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.3</note>. Elsewhere, referring to the same channels, it says: "Having moved through them, he rests in the <term>purītat</term> <gloss>pericardium or membrane surrounding the heart</gloss>" <note>Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.19</note>. Similarly, elsewhere after mentioning the channels: "In them he then remains when, being asleep, he sees no dream; then he becomes one with this <term>prāṇa</term> <gloss>vital breath/life-force</gloss> alone." In another place: "He sleeps in the space within the heart." In another: "Then, my dear, he is united with the Existent, he has gone to his own Self." And: "Embraced by the Intelligent Self, he knows nothing without and nothing within."

On this point, a doubt arises: are these locations—the channels and so forth—distinct and independent places for deep sleep, or are they mutually related parts of a single location for deep sleep? What is the initial view? That they are distinct. Why? Because they serve the same purpose—and things that serve the same purpose are never mutually dependent...

<summary>Shankara explains that the soul's divine powers are hidden by its association with the body and ignorance, meaning dreams are illusory and not creations of the soul's will. The text then transitions to discussing the location of the soul during deep sleep (susupti) based on various Upanishadic passages.</summary>
<keywords>jiva, Ishvara, dream state, deep sleep, suşupti, maya, subtle channels, nadis, ignorance, avidya</keywords>

## From that, the speed of mind, existence without instruments, and mastery over the primary cause. <note>Yoga Sutra 3.48</note>

The body's attainment of unsurpassed speed of movement is <term>manojavitva</term> <gloss>speed of mind</gloss>. The attainment of functioning by the senses of the bodiless ones, independent of a specific place, time, or object, is <term>vikaraṇabhāva</term> <gloss>existence without instruments</gloss>. Mastery over all transformations of nature is <term>pradhānajaya</term> <gloss>mastery over the primary cause</gloss>. These three accomplishments are called <term>madhupratīkā</term> <gloss>honey-like</gloss>. These are attained from the mastery over the five forms of the instruments <note>the senses</note>.

## For one who is established in the discernment of the difference between the intellect and the self, there is supremacy over all states of being and omniscience. <note>Yoga Sutra 3.49</note>

For the pure intellect <note>sattva</note> whose stains of passion <note>rajas</note> and inertia <note>tamas</note> have been washed away, existing in the highest clarity and the highest state of self-mastery, established in the mere discernment of the difference between the intellect <note>sattva</note> and the self <note>puruṣa</note>, there is supremacy over all states of being. The qualities <note>guṇas</note> which constitute the self of all things...

---

He describes the accomplishments arising from the mastery over the five forms of the senses: **From that, the speed of mind, existence without instruments, and mastery over the primary cause.** <term>Vikaraṇabhāva</term> is the instrumental functioning of the senses even for those without physical bodies. Place refers to regions like Kashmir and others. Time refers to the past and so forth. Object refers to the subtle and so forth. Through the mastery of the senses in their generic aspect <note>anvaya</note>, there is mastery over all transformations of nature, which is <term>pradhānajaya</term>. These accomplishments are called "honey-like" by those well-versed in the yoga scriptures. It might be asked: through the mastery of the senses, let the senses and their objects be mastered, but what does that have to do with their causes, such as the primary cause <note>pradhāna</note>? To this he says: **And these...** from the mastery of the five forms of the instruments, the senses, such as perception and the rest. This is what is meant: these accomplishments do not come from the mastery of the senses alone, but from the five forms, and the primary cause and others are included within that.

These meditations <note>saṃyamas</note> are the causes of power in the form of knowledge and action. Through the door of faith produced by the conclusion of their own accomplishments, he shows the intermediate powers of that for whose sake they exist—the discernment of the difference between the intellect and the self: **For one who is established in the discernment of the difference between the intellect and the self, there is supremacy over all states of being and omniscience.** Clarity comes from having the stains of passion and inertia washed away; from that comes the higher state of self-mastery. Indeed, the mind-intellect <note>citta-sattva</note> when overwhelmed by passion and inertia was not under control; however, when these are subsided, it is under the control of the yogi who has mastery. For that yogi who has mastery and is established in the mere discernment of the difference between the intellect and the self, there is supremacy over all states of being. He explains this very point: **The qualities which constitute the self of all...**

<meta>This page contains commentaries on Chapter 48 and the beginning of Chapter 49 of the Tao Te Ching. The commentators include Su Zhe (Su Zhu), Lü Huiqing (Lü Zhu), Huang Maocai, and Xizhai (Li Jia).</meta>

<margin>Su's Commentary <note>Su Zhe, 1039–1112 AD, a prominent Song dynasty official and scholar.</note></margin> Those who do not know the <term>Dao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but devote themselves to learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily. Without a single principle to unify this knowledge, they cannot avoid it becoming a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it. This is the second level of knowledge." <note>A reference to the Analects 7:27.</note> If one day a person knows the <term>Dao</term>, they will look back at their previous false actions and realize that none were not delusions. Removing delusions to return to one's true nature is called "decreasing." Confucius asked Zigong: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" Zigong replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with a single thread." <note>Reference to Analects 15:3. The "single thread" implies a unifying spiritual principle rather than an accumulation of facts.</note> Forgetting the mind to return purely to one's nature is what is meant by "decreasing." If delusions still remain, one must continue until both the delusions and the act of forgetting are themselves forgotten. Once the mind returns purely to nature without any remainder, then one eliminates "doing" <note>purposive, ego-driven action</note> and does not fail to reach <term>wu wei</term> <gloss>non-action or effortless action</gloss>. All people have the desire to take hold of the world and finish its affairs; thus, they create business and seek after things. When their intentions are visible externally, things <note>others, or the world at large</note> will dislike them, making success difficult. The Sage practices non-action and therefore has no "business" in his heart. When his heart is visible externally, things are at peace with him. Although he does not try to take hold of the world's affairs, the world's affairs naturally follow and find peace through him.

<margin>Lü's Commentary <note>Lü Huiqing, 1032–1111 AD, a key figure in the New Policies of the Song dynasty.</note></margin> Practicing learning is for those who have not yet heard the <term>Dao</term>. Seeking it without having heard it requires breadth, hence it is said "one gains daily." Practicing the <term>Dao</term> is for those who have already heard the <term>Dao</term>. Having heard it and acting upon it requires nothing more than non-action, hence it is said "one decreases daily." To "decrease and further decrease" means one has not yet escaped the realm of "doing." Only by decreasing even the act of decreasing does one arrive at <term>wu wei</term> <gloss>non-action</gloss>. Non-action refers to being still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" refers to being moved and subsequently penetrating the causes of all under heaven. Arriving at non-action through the process of non-action is what is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called divine; the direction of the divine is what is called the <term>Dao</term>. As for the ultimate divine, who can compare to this? From this perspective, taking the world is always done through non-action. As for using "doing" <note>purposive action</note>, it is clear that this is insufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Huang Maocai's Commentary <note>A Southern Song dynasty scholar known for his work on the Laozi.</note></margin> Only after there is nothing one does not know can one speak of learning; therefore, learning desires a daily increase. Only after there is nothing one does not do can one speak of the <term>Dao</term>; therefore, the <term>Dao</term> desires a daily decrease. However, increase can be sought through progress, while decrease is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly drop everything and reach the realm of non-action. Thus they can leave nothing undone, and their practical application is inexhaustible, applied to the world with great ease.

<margin>Xizhai's Commentary <note>Li Jia, also known by his pseudonym Xizhai.</note></margin> Practicing learning is the means to seek knowledge, so it increases daily. Practicing the <term>Dao</term> is the means to remove delusion, so it decreases daily. If knowledge is not ultimate, then the decrease will not be complete. Thus, daily increase serves as the foundation for daily decrease. If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is whole, then one reaches non-action. When one reaches non-action, then every instance of "doing" is never anything other than "non-doing." This state cannot easily be discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When non-action reaches its ultimate point, even with the vastness of the world, one unifies it with a single thread. If one uses "busyness" <note>interfering action</note> to create more business, then even a single object beforehand will be sticky, entangled, and wrong, let alone the vastness of the world.

The Sage has no fixed heart <note>or mind</note>; he takes the heart of the people as his own. Those who are good, I treat as good. In ancient times, the Son of Heaven <note>the Emperor</note> had a thousand officials and the feudal lords had a hundred officials. When a ruler used these thousand officials to make his commands effective throughout all the Chinese states, he was called a King. When a ruler used these hundred officials to make his commands effective within his own borders, even if the state was not entirely peaceful, it did not reach the point of collapsing or losing its hereditary succession <gloss>original: "falling or being exchanged," interpreted as losing the ancestral line</gloss> <margin>The character for "falling" is read as "to drop," meaning to lose one's professional legacy.</margin>; such a ruler was called a Lord. 

Consider the son of a Sage King. After he inherits the world, he possesses the official records of the land and occupies the position of the head of the Great House of the world. However, if he is without talent and is not upright <margin>Not "middle" means not being middle-and-upright.</margin>, then internally the common people will hate him, and externally the feudal lords will rebel against him. Those near him within his borders will not be unified, and those far away among the feudal lords will not obey. His commands will not even be followed within his own territory. In extreme cases, the feudal lords will encroach upon his land, diminish his territory, and launch military attacks against him. If things reach this state, even if he has not yet perished, I say he no longer "possesses the world."

When a Sage King dies and his successor is weak and unfit for duty <margin>The character for "tired" is pronounced like "pi," meaning weak and incapable of handling affairs. "Suspend" means to keep the world tied or connected to the ruler.</margin>, such that he cannot hold the world together, the world is effectively without a ruler. If among the feudal lords there is one whose virtue is brilliant and whose majesty has accumulated, so that none among the people within the four seas <note>the known world</note> does not wish to have him as their ruler and teacher, yet a violent state remains arrogant and unrestrained <margin>A "violent state" refers to those like the tyrants Jie and Zhou. "Uniquely extravagant" means acting with total license. The word "how" here functions as "then."</margin>, then that leader must be able to punish them. He must not harm the innocent people. Executing the ruler of a violent state is like executing a "lone man" <margin>A "lone man" refers to one whom the whole world has abandoned, leaving him like a single individual without support.</margin>. If he acts in this way, he can be said to be able to "employ the world." One who can employ the world is called a King.

The Kings Tang and Wu did not "seize" the world. They cultivated the Way and practiced righteousness. They shared the same interests as the world and eliminated the common harms of the world, and thus the world turned to them. The tyrants Jie and Zhou did not "lose" the world <margin>This implies the world left them of its own accord.</margin>. It shows that the statement of the superiority of each successive thing over the preceding one is for that [realization] alone. This is what is meant by "furthermore." The author of the Sutras connects the phrase "for the sake of the narrative" by explaining that the superiority of objects and the rest is taught as a prelude to the vision of the <term>Purusha</term>, as there is no independent purpose for them. (14) Regarding "And because of the word Atman": moreover, since there is consistency between the beginning and the end in passages such as "That is the highest step of Vishnu" and "There is nothing higher than the Purusha," it is established that the entire text forms a single coherent idea focused on the one <term>Purusha</term> who possesses the fruit [of liberation]. Therefore, it is not proper to assume a division of the text or a division of the results, as that would be unnecessarily complex. (15)

->**Nyaya Nirnaya**<-

"For what reason?" asks the text. Thinking that there is no result from knowing the superiority of things other than the object of primary intent, the author says, "because of a lack of purpose." Anticipating the question of how a lack of purpose can be asserted, he rejects the idea that the result is either established by worldly presence and absence or by scripture. He says, "No." Regarding the second part, he says, "it is not heard." Since this context is seen to concern reality, it is not proper to view it as a command for meditation. Since it is possible for it to concern the knowledge of the truth of the supreme goal of man, it is not proper for the senses and the rest, which are established in memory, to concern some other human goal. This means the knowledge of each individual part is not established as the primary intent. Even if the knowledge of the superiority of the <term>Purusha</term> were not fruitful, how could the knowledge of the superiority of the senses, etc., which is an inference, lead to the human goal? Anticipating this, he says that the desire for the superiority of the <term>Purusha</term> is never destroyed, because it has as its object that which is unconditioned and devoid of objects. He says, "In the Purusha, however..." Thinking that it is not proper to imagine an unseen result when the destruction of ignorance and false knowledge is a seen result, he says, "it is seen." To one who disputes the experience of the wise, he cites scripture to show that the vision of the superiority of the <term>Purusha</term> has a seen result: "Thus also..." For another reason why this entire context has the knowledge of the <term>Purusha</term> as its primary intent, he says, "Furthermore..." By the sign of prohibition "Higher than the Purusha [there is nothing]" and by the word "pinnacle" <note>kastha</note>, the Veda shows its regard for the subject of the <term>Purusha</term>. The "sequence of preceding and succeeding" refers to the statement of the superiority of each successive thing over the preceding. Since a command for meditation is absent here, how can the knowledge of the Supreme Person be for the sake of meditation? Anticipating this, he explains the part of the Sutra: "narrative." Even the knowledge of the <term>Brahman</term> without qualities is for the sake of meditation because it resides in <term>Brahman</term>; but as it describes the one with qualities, he states the contradiction with the scripture "Then indeed him..." by saying, "Perfect..." (14) He gives another reason why the <term>Purusha</term> alone is the subject here due to its superiority over all: "And the word Atman." He explains the "and" in the Sutra: "For this reason also..." Clarifying that, he analyzes the word "Atman": "That..." He wards off the doubt that the non-manifestation of the Self is natural by saying, "It is seen, however." He says that in that very scripture, the word <term>Atman</term> is used: "the subject under discussion." He states the intended meaning of the explanation of the terms in the Sutra: "And from this..." He establishes the remaining prior meaning: "its..." He states the intent of the latter meaning: "refined." He states another reason indicated by the "and": "that." Restraining speech and the rest is what is understood in the mantra, not a rule for meditation; he says "it has been explained." Because the scripture itself states that the Self and the meaning of the scripture are difficult to know due to the repetition of unknown meanings, and since the senses and the rest are easy to understand, the statement of their superiority is also for the purpose of the primary intent. Thus, the excellence of the intent between the beginning and the end...

<summary>This page argues that the hierarchy of senses and objects in the Upanishads is not meant to teach their individual importance, but to direct the seeker toward the Supreme Person (Purusha) and the Self (Atman). Realizing this supreme reality is the only path to liberation (Moksha).</summary>

A courtesan who refuses to go to a man authorized by the king’s command shall receive one thousand lashes with a whip, or pay a fine of five thousand <term>panas</term> <gloss>the standard silver coin of the period</gloss>.

If a courtesan, after accepting payment for enjoyment, shows hatred or refuses the client, she shall be fined twice the amount of the payment.

If she steals the payment or denies a client lodging after accepting payment, she shall pay eight times the amount as a fine, unless the client suffers from a disease or possesses personal defects.

If a courtesan causes injury or suffering to a man she is excessively dependent upon, she shall be punished by being drowned in water.

Anyone who steals a courtesan's ornaments or her payment for enjoyment shall be fined eight times the value.

The courtesan shall report her earnings, her future income, and the identity of her clients to the authorities.

By these rules, the legal dealings concerning the wives of actors, dancers, singers, musicians, storytellers, bards, rope-dancers, jugglers, and wandering performers, as well as women who live in secret through prostitution, are explained.

Foreign musical troupes arriving for performances shall pay five <term>panas</term> as a performance license fee.

<meta>continues from the previous page: discussion of the impartiality of God regarding His devotees.</meta>

<note>Commentary by Sridhara Swami:</note>
If you grant liberation only to devotees and not to non-devotees, does that not imply you possess partiality born of attachment and aversion? He answers this in the negative with the verse beginning with "I am equal." I am equal toward all beings; therefore, to Me, there is no one particularly dear or hateful. Even so, those who worship Me with devotion, those devotees abide in Me, and I also abide in them as their benefactor. The idea is this: just as fire removes the distress of darkness and cold only for those who serve <note>stay near</note> it, yet the fire itself possesses no partiality; or just as a wish-fulfilling tree <term>kalpavriksha</term> <gloss>a divine tree that grants all desires</gloss> acts similarly; in the same way, although I favor My devotees, I have no partiality. Rather, this is the glorious power of devotion to Me. (Verse 29)

<note>Commentary by Madhusudana Sarasvati:</note>
Furthermore, listen to the greatness of devotion to Me, which creates the appearance of partiality even in One who is equal:

> Even if a man of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion,
> he must be considered righteous, for he has rightly resolved. (Verse 30)

If anyone, even one of very wicked conduct like <term>Ajamila</term> <gloss>a legendary sinner who was saved by calling the name of God at death</gloss> and others, worships Me with undivided devotion due to some dawn of good fortune, he must be considered righteous, even if he was unrighteous before. This is because <note>as the text says "hi"</note> he has rightly resolved; he possesses the firm conviction of a saint. (Verse 30)

<note>Commentary by Sridhara Swami:</note>
Showing that the influence of devotion to Me is inconceivable, He says "Even if": Even a man of extremely wicked conduct, if he worships Me, Lord Narayana, without practicing devotion to other deities separately, then he must be considered as someone excellent <note>a saint</note>. Because he has "rightly resolved"—he has made the beautiful determination that "I shall achieve my life's purpose simply by worshiping the Supreme Lord." (Verse 30)

<note>Commentary by Madhusudana Sarasvati:</note>
Because of this right resolution, having abandoned his wicked conduct:

> Quickly he becomes a righteous soul and attains eternal peace.
> O son of Kunti <note>Arjuna</note>, know for certain: My devotee never perishes. (Verse 31)

Even if he was an unrighteous soul for a long time, through the greatness of worshiping Me, he "quickly"—very soon—becomes a righteous soul <term>dharmatma</term> <gloss>one whose mind follows virtue</gloss>. The meaning is that by immediately abandoning wicked conduct, he becomes a man of good conduct. Furthermore, he "attains eternal peace"—he completely reaches the cessation of the desire for sense objects through extreme detachment. To the doubt that "some devotee of Mine might not become a righteous soul because he does not give up previously practiced wicked conduct, and thus he might perish," the Lord says "No," as if He were angry out of His extreme compassion for His devotees: "O son of Kunti, do not think this is a wonder; such is the greatness of devotion to Me. Therefore, even in the presence of those who disagree, you should declare it; make a proud and bold proclamation: 'The devotee of Me, Vasudeva, even if he is very wicked in conduct, even if his life is in danger, even if he is sought after for something very rare, even if he is a complete fool or without refuge, he never perishes; rather, he achieves his life's purpose.'"

<summary>The text explains that God is impartial toward all, but devotion creates a special bond that redeems even the most wicked sinners. It emphasizes that a firm resolve to worship God quickly transforms an individual's character and ensures they never perish spiritually.</summary>

( 1 ) **Medhātithi:** The previously mentioned fault does not apply here. Slaughter ordained by the Vedas and Law-codes as a part of a sacrifice is for the sake of bringing about prosperity. Animals were created—produced—by the Self-Existent One, Prajāpati. The phrase "himself" is an explanatory praise <note>original: <term>arthavāda</term></note>. Therefore, the killing that occurs there is to be understood as "non-killing." This is said to indicate the absence of the sin that normally arises from violence. ( 39 )

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** He removes the doubt as to why such a fault does not exist in ritual killing. Sacrifice is for the "prosperity" of the world, meaning its birth; through the sequence of the offering reaching the Sun, which brings rain, which produces seeds, which leads to the production of semen, and finally the birth of living beings. By this, it is said that through the ritual slaughter of one animal, many living beings are sustained, and thus no such fault exists. ( 39 )

## Section 4: On Sealed Deposits <note>original: "उपनिधिप्रकरणम्"</note>

The depositary shall not be compelled to pay for a <term>upanidhi</term> <gloss>sealed deposit</gloss> if it is stolen by thieves, lost through acts of God <note>such as fire or floods</note>, or seized by the King. The loss of that property belongs to the owner alone, provided there was no <term>jihma-karita</term> <gloss>fraudulent action or negligence</gloss> involved. As **Narada** says: "If the property is lost together with the property of the receiver, the loss is the giver's; likewise if it is caused by Fate <note>acts of God</note> or the King, provided it was not caused by fraud."

He <note>Yajnavalkya</note> states an exception to this:

### If loss occurs when the deposit was requested but not returned, the depositary must pay the value and an equal fine. (66)

If the depositary does not return the property when it is <term>margite</term> <gloss>sought or requested</gloss> by the owner, and if subsequently a <term>bhresha</term> <gloss>loss or destruction</gloss> occurs even through the King or other causes, the receiver must pay the value of that property to the owner and an equal amount as a fine to the King. (66)

He states the punishment for one who uses the deposit:

### One who makes a living from the deposit of his own accord shall be fined and must return it with interest.

One who, of his own will and without the owner's permission, <term>ajivan</term> <gloss>lives off or makes a living from</gloss> the deposited property — meaning he uses it or employs it in trade for profit — shall be fined according to the extent of the enjoyment or the profit made. He must return that <term>upanidhi</term> <gloss>sealed deposit</gloss> to the owner <term>sodayam</term> <gloss>with interest</gloss>: with interest if it was consumed, and with the profit if it was used in trade. The rate of interest is stated by **Katyayana**: "If a person does not return a <term>nikshepa</term> <gloss>open deposit</gloss>, the remainder of a debt, or goods bought or sold when requested, it shall increase by five percent <note>per month</note>." This should be understood as applying when the item is "consumed" <note>used up</note>. In cases of loss through neglect or ignorance, the same author <note>Katyayana</note> shows a distinction: "If consumed, it must be paid back with interest; if lost through neglect, the original amount must be paid; if lost through ignorance, the amount paid back should be slightly less." "Slightly less" means reduced by one-fourth.

He extends the rules of the sealed deposit to requested items and other categories:

### This rule applies to requested items, secondary deposits, trusts, open deposits, and the like. (67)

**Yachita** <gloss>requested item</gloss> refers to clothes, ornaments, and the like, borrowed for ceremonies such as weddings. When property is placed in the hands of one person, and he later places it in the hand of another saying, "Give this to the owner," that is an **anvahita** <gloss>secondary deposit</gloss>. **Nyasa** <gloss>trust</gloss> refers to the act of placing property in the hands of a member of a household in the absence of the master, without showing it to the master, with the intent that it be handed over to him. Handing it over in the master's presence is a **nikshepa** <gloss>open deposit</gloss>. The word "and the like" <note>adi</note> includes gold and such given to a goldsmith for making bracelets, as well as a <term>pratinyasa</term> <gloss>mutual deposit</gloss>, where for mutual benefit one says, "This of mine is to be protected by you, and this of yours is protected by me." As **Narada** says: "This same rule is seen for requested items, secondary deposits, and the like; and likewise for the work of artisans, sealed deposits, trusts, and mutual deposits." In these cases — requested items, secondary deposits, etc. — this rule, which is the rule of return and liability for a sealed deposit, should be understood. (67)

#### I. Identification
**There are six kinds of defiled minds.**

#### II. Inquiry
**What are the six?**

These six defilements are correlated in reverse order with the six coarse characteristics and the three subtle characteristics mentioned earlier <note>from the Awakening of Faith</note>. The first four of these six correspond to the third and fourth coarse characteristics; therefore, there are only six in total. These names are borrowed to categorize these six types.

**First is the "Attachment-Associated Defilement." It is distanced by the liberation of the Two Vehicles <note>the Hearers and the Solitary Realizers</note> and by the Ground of Faith-Association. This corresponds to the third and fourth of the six coarse characteristics.**

Question: For what causes and conditions was this treatise composed?

The answer consists of three parts: stating the number, explaining the characteristics, and the final summary.

Answer: There are eight kinds of causes and conditions. What are these eight?

In the explanation of the characteristics, the first is general and the following seven are specific. The reason for this is that the general covers both the primary and secondary objectives, while the specific ones address those individuals who are ready for the teaching; thus, it must be so.

1. The general characteristic of the causes and conditions: namely, to cause all sentient beings to leave behind all suffering and obtain ultimate bliss.

Within the general characteristic, "leaving behind all suffering" means causing sentient beings to leave behind the three types of suffering <note>The three types are: suffering from pain itself, suffering from the change of pleasant things, and suffering from the conditioned nature of existence.</note> and the two types of death <note>The two types are: "fragmentary death" involving physical rebirth and "transformational death" which is the subtle rebirth experienced by advanced practitioners.</note>. Consequently, "obtaining ultimate bliss" means causing them to obtain the bliss of Supreme Enlightenment <note>original: "Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi"</note> and Great Nirvana <note>original: "Mahaparinirvana"</note>. This is not for seeking worldly fame and profit. There are two interpretations of this: first, it is not intended to make them seek the benefits and happiness of human or heavenly realms in future lives.

### Zixia said: "One who treats the worthy as worthy and thereby changes his love of sensual beauty; who, in serving his parents, can exert his full strength; who, in serving his prince, can devote his life; and who, in interacting with friends, is trustworthy in his words — even if it is said that such a person has not yet studied, I would certainly call him a man of learning."

Zixia was a disciple of Confucius. His surname was Bu and his given name was Shang; he was a man of the state of Wei. To "treat the worthy as worthy and change sensual beauty" <term>xian xian yi se</term> means to honor the virtue of worthy people and thereby replace the desire for physical beauty. It refers to having a sincere love for the good. The Collected Commentaries <note>referring to the *Lunyu Jizhu* by Zhu Xi</note> state that seeing worthiness changes the expression of the face <note>the "color"</note> to show a love for goodness. Master Zhu said that the Master twice remarked on never seeing anyone who loved virtue as much as they loved sensual beauty. The *Doctrine of the Mean* also considers distancing oneself from beauty as a method for self-cultivation. To "devote" <term>zhi</term> means to give over or entrust. Devoting one's body <note>or life</note> means not holding onto one's self interest. This sincerity in replacing the love of beauty is why Fan’s explanation is considered superior.

### The Master said: "A gentleman has no cause for contention. If he must, is it not in archery? They bow and yield to one another as they ascend, and as they descend to drink. Such is the contention of a gentleman." <note>The word for "gentleman" is pronounced in the departing tone.</note>

"Bowing and yielding as they ascend" refers to the ritual of the Great Archery. This "bowing as they advance" involves performing three bows before ascending to the hall. <note>Note from Mr. Hu</note>
In the ritual of archery, the Master of Archery forms three pairs of archers. The three pairs emerge from the waiting area, face west, and bow. When they reach the north of the steps, they bow. Upon reaching the steps, they bow again. This is what is meant by "performing three bows before ascending to the hall."

This refers to bowing as they descend after the archery is finished to wait for the other pairs. Once all pairs have descended, the winner bows to the loser, and the loser ascends the hall to take the <term>jue</term> <gloss>ritual wine cup</gloss>.

"Subhuti, what do you think? If someone were to fill three thousand great thousand-fold worlds with the seven treasures <note>traditionally gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, agate, ruby, and cornelian</note> and give them all in an act of <term>dana</term> <gloss>generous giving</gloss>, would this person gain much merit from such a cause?"

Subhuti replied: "Indeed, World-Honored One. This person would gain very much merit from such a cause."

"Subhuti, if merit had a substantial reality, the Tathagata <note>an epithet of the Buddha meaning 'One who has thus come'</note> would not say that the merit gained is much. It is because merit is without substance that the Tathagata says the merit gained is much."

<note>Huineng's commentary:</note> The merit of the seven treasures cannot achieve the fruit of Buddhahood and <term>Bodhi</term> <gloss>Enlightenment</gloss>, therefore it is said to be "nothing." Because it is limitless and beyond number, it is called "much." If one can transcend this, then one does not speak of "much."
